card.summary: Fast Lane access offers up to 50,000 GPU hours for a maximum of three months, with approval within four working days on a rolling first-in-first-out basis an...

free_tier.stated: Fast Lane access offers up to 50,000 GPU hours for a maximum of three months, with approval within four working days on a rolling first-in-first-out basis and expert support from the hosting AI Factory; Playground access sits below it for entry-level users.

record.interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
record.chaining: Playground access is explicitly pitched as the way to gather the technical data that a Fast Lane or Large Scale application needs, so the two tiers form a ladder from a small test to 50,000 GPU hours, provided the applicant is a company.

limits.value: The call requires the applicant organisation to prove its status with a valid VAT number and a Participant Identification Code, and requires the PI to hold an employment contract in that organisation, which excludes a person with no registered company.

record.limits_note: The call requires the applicant organisation to prove its status with a valid VAT number and a Participant Identification Code, and requires the PI to hold an employment contract in that organisation, which excludes a person with no registered company.
record.binding_note: The call requires the applicant organisation to prove its status with a valid VAT number and a Participant Identification Code, and requires the PI to hold an employment contract in that organisation, which excludes a person with no registered company.

deadline model multiple cut-off, roughly two per month from 30 Jan 2026 through 4 Jan 2027, quoted

AI Factory call table: Playground '<= 5,000' GPU hours, Fast Lane '5,001 - 50,000', Large Scale '> 50,000', published by the LUMI hosting entity
'Applications will be processed in the order they are received. There is no competitive selection process and access can be granted within two working days'; allocations for 1, 2 or 3 months, quoted

record.notes: This is the largest single GPU-hour number found that is not gated on peer-reviewed science: 50,000 GPU hours, four working days, no competitive selection. earlier readings already holds a storage-side row rejecting Playground access as 'industry only' with verdict fails-quota; that row is not wrong but it records no number. The binding constraint here is not the industry framing, it is the VAT number and PIC, which is the concrete thing a single person lacks. Classified as fails-identity rather than fails-quota because the size is not the objection. The Playground per-application GPU-hour cap is published only in a system table that did not render through automated retrieval, so it is null here.

card.summary: A continuously open call with monthly cut-offs, giving a limited number of node hours for code scalability tests or AI application tests before applying for ...

free_tier.stated: A continuously open call with monthly cut-offs, giving a limited number of node hours for code scalability tests or AI application tests before applying for Regular or Extreme Scale access; the maximum allocation period is three months, with a maximum time-to-resources-access of two to three weeks.

record.interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
record.chaining: The benchmark result is designed to feed a Regular or Extreme Scale proposal, so the tier's real value is the scaling data it produces, not the node hours.

limits.value: The benchmark tier is the cheapest door in the EuroHPC stack, but it is still awarded through a proposal evaluated by the Access Resource Committee, and the call text targets researchers and HPC application developers established in an EU Member State or a Horizon-associated country.

record.provider: EuroHPC JU Regular Access (LUMI, Leonardo, MareNostrum 5, JUPITER)

free_tier.stated: LUMI-O object storage: 150 TB default quota per project, expandable up to 2.1 PB, retained for the project lifetime, billing rate 0.25x.
free_tier.notes: Access to EuroHPC systems is free of charge.

retention.stated: LUMI-O object storage is retained for the project lifetime.

egress.terms: Free for allocation holders within the facility; object storage endpoints (LUMI-O S3) are internet-reachable.

record.tooling: LUMI-O is S3-compatible (rclone 's3'); other sites expose Lustre/POSIX plus Globus.
record.chaining: Storage comes attached to a compute award, so a storage-heavy proposal can be packaged inside a modest compute request. One-year allocations with successive cut-offs allow re-application.

limits.value: allocations are granted for one (1) year

record.limits_note: Geography is the hard gate: eligibility is limited to entities 'established or located in an EU Member State or in a Participating State or in a third country associated to the Digital Europe Programme or to Horizon Europe'. The published country list runs to ~45 states (incl. Turkiye, Tunisia, Ukraine, Georgia, Armenia, Israel, UK) and excludes everyone else. Allocations are one year; ~4 months from cut-off to access.

identity_cost.detail: Applicants must be researchers from academia, research institutes, public authorities or industry established or located in an EU Member State, a Participating State or a third country associated to the Digital Europe Programme or to Horizon Europe.

record.reliability_note: Well-run; the constraint is purely eligibility and the compute-justification burden.
record.confidence_note: Documented from vendor pages re-read on 2026-11-04: https://docs.lumi-supercomputer.eu/storage/ (LUMI-O 150 TB, project lifetime), https://www.eurohpc-ju.europa.eu/supercomputers/supercomputers-access-policy-and-faq_en (free of charge; eligibility) and https://www.eurohpc-ju.europa.eu/eurohpc-ju-call-proposals-regular-access-mode_en (one-year allocations).

card.summary: PRACE no longer runs its own access calls; at the end of 2022 the EuroHPC JU took over management of the peer-review and support process, and the PRACE site ...

free_tier.stated: PRACE no longer runs its own access calls; at the end of 2022 the EuroHPC JU took over management of the peer-review and support process, and the PRACE site now serves an archive of calls that closed in 2023.

record.interface_detail: inferred from the tooling the provider documents; not probed
record.chaining: PRACE's review machinery is the same machinery now operating the EuroHPC calls, so its successor is the EuroHPC Benchmark, Development, Regular and Extreme Scale set recorded elsewhere in documented records.
record.limits_note: There is nothing left to apply for: the programme's allocation function moved into the EuroHPC JU, so the successor question is answered by the EuroHPC rows rather than by a PRACE row.
record.binding_note: There is nothing left to apply for: the programme's allocation function moved into the EuroHPC JU, so the successor question is answered by the EuroHPC rows rather than by a PRACE row.

evidence.proved: 'At the end of 2022, the EuroHPC JU, as owner of an increasing number of world-class European supercomputers, took over from PRACE the management of this peer-review and support process', quoted
PRACE's Regular Access page lists its last open call as the 2023-07-07 cut-off and files every later item under 'Closed Calls'

record.notes: The answer is that the successor is not a separate brand: it is the EuroHPC JU, which absorbed PRACE's peer-review process at the end of 2022. No quota is recorded because there is no live call. Identity cost is recorded as 'none' rather than a normal vocabulary value, because a withdrawn programme has no applicant and no identity to produce; recording 'institution' here would imply a door that no longer exists.
